name: Hip abduction
pattern: Leg moves out to the side against resistance, lying, seated, standing or stepping, to train the side hip.
setup: Lie on your side, bottom knee bent for support, top leg straight in line with your body.
Stack your hips: the top hip directly over the bottom one, not rolled back.
Toes of the top leg point forward, not up.

steps.text: Top leg resting on the bottom one, hips stacked.
Raise the straight leg up and slightly back, heel leading.
Stop at about 35-45°, hold a second.
Lower slowly without letting the leg rest.

cues.cue: Keep your hips stacked; do not roll back.
cues.why: Rolling back turns the lift into hip flexion, which uses the front hip muscles instead of the glute medius.

cues.cue: Toes forward, heel leads, leg slightly behind you.
cues.why: Turning the toes up shifts work to the tensor fascia lata and hip flexors.
Lifting higher only bends the trunk sideways; the side-lying lift already gives the highest glute medius activity of common exercises.

cues.cue: Slow lift, 1-2 second hold, slow lower.
cues.why: Control keeps the side hip working through the whole rep.

breathing: Breathe out as the leg lifts, in as it lowers.

tempo.note: Lift in 1 second, hold 1, lower in 2.

mistakes.name: Hips roll back
mistakes.looks: The top hip rolls behind the bottom one and the toes turn up to the ceiling.
mistakes.fix: Stack your hips, toes forward; lie with your back against a wall.
mistakes.why: The lift becomes hip flexion with rotation, done by the front hip muscles.

mistakes.name: Leg drifts forward
mistakes.looks: The lifting leg moves in front of the body line.
mistakes.fix: Keep the leg in line with your body or slightly behind it.
mistakes.why: A leg in front lets the hip flexors and TFL take over.

mistakes.name: Lifting too high
mistakes.looks: The leg swings high and the waist crunches sideways.
mistakes.why: Past the hip's range the trunk side-bends to fake height.

safety: Hip pain on the side you lie on: put a pillow under it or do the standing version.
Lower-back pain: keep the trunk still and the range smaller.

variants.change: Band above the knees or at the ankles: band at the feet is harder.
Extra load on the leg: same keyframes.
Kneeling on one knee with a cable at the free ankle.
Push the knees out against a band or pad while holding a squat.

subtypes.name: Clam
subtypes.change: Side-lying with hips about 45° and knees about 90° bent, feet together; lift the top knee by turning the thigh out.

subtypes.name: Seated abduction (machine or band)
subtypes.change: Seated, hips and knees 90°, push both knees out against the pads or a band.

subtypes.name: Standing abduction
subtypes.change: Stand on one leg holding a support; move the other leg out to the side with the trunk upright.

subtypes.name: Lateral band walk
subtypes.change: Band around the legs, small half squat, step sideways keeping tension; knees stay out. Loop: cycle.

motion.basis: Default is side-lying straight-leg abduction on the left side, right leg lifting (body is horizontal; joint angles are relative to the trunk). Top height about 45° from aaos-knee; glute medius ranking from distefano2009; position faults from selkowitz2013. Angles otherwise estimated.

sources.cite: Distefano LJ, Blackburn JT, Marshall SW, Padua DA. Gluteal muscle activation during common therapeutic exercises. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2009;39(7):532-540.

Selkowitz DM, Beneck GJ, Powers CM. Which exercises target the gluteal muscles while minimizing activation of the tensor fascia lata? Electromyographic assessment using fine-wire electrodes. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2013;43(2):54-64.
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Knee conditioning program. OrthoInfo. Accessed 2026-10-23.
